## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** Native mobile accessibility as a design decision, plus the current legal enforcement landscape for digital accessibility. Narrow scope — two related halves. HALF ONE, native platform accessibility that a DESIGNER must decide, not a developer: (1) Apple Dynamic Type — the text style ramp, what sizes the accessibility sizes reach, what a designer must commit to for a layout to survive the largest accessibility text sizes, and Apple's stated guidance on layouts that must reflow or switch to vertical at large sizes; (2) VoiceOver on iOS — accessibility traits, labels vs hints vs values, the rotor and heading structure, what a designer decides about reading order and grouping; (3) Android TalkBack and the Android accessibility model — content descriptions, touch exploration, the recommended 48dp target and its relationship to WCAG, and Android's font scaling including non-linear font scaling introduced in Android 14; (4) what accessibility requirements differ between native and web such that a web-derived checklist misses them entirely. HALF TWO, legal drivers and their CURRENT enforcement state as of 2026: (5) the European Accessibility Act (Directive EU 2019/882) — what became applicable in June 2025, exactly which products and services are in scope, the microenterprise exemption and its thresholds, and what standard conformance is measured against (EN 301 549 and its relationship to WCAG); (6) the US DOJ ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR part 35 subpart H) — the technical standard it names, and its compliance deadlines by public entity size; (7) Section 508 and what standard it currently references; (8) whether any binding instrument yet names WCAG 2.2 rather than 2.1 or 2.0. Prioritize primary sources only: developer.apple.com Human Interface Guidelines accessibility pages, developer.android.com accessibility docs, EUR-Lex official directive text, ada.gov and the Federal Register, and the ETSI EN 301 549 standard text. Reject law-firm marketing blogs and accessibility-vendor content marketing where a primary source exists.

6 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] Apple's iOS/iPadOS Dynamic Type ramp has 7 standard sizes (xSmall through xxxLarge, default = Large) plus 5 larger accessibility sizes AX1-AX5, and the Body text style scales from 17pt at the default to 53pt at AX5 - roughly 3.1x. Large Title runs 34pt to 60pt over the same range.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography (primary)
Quote: "Large (default) … Body | Regular | 17 | 22 | Semibold … iOS, iPadOS larger accessibility type sizes … AX5 … Body | Regular | 53 | 62 | Semibold"
Verifier evidence (high): Tried to refute; every number checks out against Apple's own data. Fetched the HIG typography page's backing DocC JSON (https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography.json — the rendered HTML page is JS-only, so WebFetch returns nothing useful) and parsed the spec tables verbatim.

(1) "7 standard sizes, default = Large": section "iOS, iPadOS Dynamic Type sizes" contains exactly 7 subsection tables — xSmall, Small, Medium, "Large (default)", xLarge, xxLarge, xxxLarge. Confirmed, including that Large is the one Apple labels default.

(2) "5 accessibility sizes AX1-AX5": a separate section titled "iOS, iPadOS larger accessibility type sizes" contains exactly 5 tables — AX1, AX2, AX3, AX4, AX5. Confirmed.

(3) "Body 17pt → 53pt, roughly 3.1x": Large (default) row = "Body | Regular | 17 | 22 | Semibold". AX5 row = "Body | Regular | 53 | 62 | Semibold". 53/17 = 3.118, so "roughly 3.1x" is accurate, not rounded favorably. The full Body ramp is 17 / 28 / 33 / 40 / 47 / 53 (Large, AX1-AX5).

(4) "Large Title 34pt → 60pt": Large (default) = "Large Title | Regular | 34 | 41 | Bold"; AX5 = "Large Title | Regular | 60 | 70 | Bold". Confirmed. (My prior expectation was 58 at AX5 — the source says 60, so the claim is right and my recollection was wrong.) Full Large Title ramp: 34 / 44 / 48 / 52 / 56 / 60.

Currency: the page's own change log lists "December 16, 2025 — Added emphasized weights to the Dynamic Type style specifications for each platform" as the most recent revision, so this is the live spec as of August 2026, not a stale table. The supporting quote in the claim ("Body | Regular | 17 | 22 | Semibold" and AX5 "Body | Regular | 53 | 62 | Semibold") reproduces the emphasized-weight column added in that Dec 2025 revision, which corroborates it was read from the current page rather than an older cached copy.

Source quality: primary (Apple, first-party normative spec). No vendor blog or law-firm content involved. WebSearch for contradicting values surfaced only secondary write-ups (Medium/UX Collective/dept engineering), none of which dispute these figures; one independently states 12 total sizes and ~310% body scaling at AX5, consistent with the claim.

Non-refuting caveat worth carrying forward into the design guidance rather than treated as an error: the scaling is not uniform across styles — Body goes 3.1x while Large Title goes only 1.76x (34→60), and at AX5 Body (53) is larger than the default Large Title (34) and nearly equal to Headline (53) and Title 3 (55). That is the actual designer-facing consequence and it strengthens rather than undercuts the claim.

### [1] Apple explicitly instructs designers to switch to a stacked (vertical) layout at large font sizes, naming inline glyphs, timestamps and container boundaries as the specific elements that crowd text and cause truncation or overlap in horizontally constrained contexts.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography (primary)
Quote: "Consider adjusting your layout at large font sizes. When font size increases in a horizontally constrained context, inline items (like glyphs and timestamps) and container boundaries can crowd text and cause truncation or overlapping. To improve readability, consider using a stacked layout where text appears above secondary items."
Verifier evidence (high): VERBATIM MATCH CONFIRMED at the primary source. WebFetch on the rendered HIG page returns only a JS shell, so I pulled Apple's own DocC data endpoint: `curl https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography.json` (HTTP 200, 279KB). Grepping it yields exactly one occurrence each of "stacked", "horizontally constrained", "timestamp", "container bound", "crowd", and "adjusting your layout", in a single paragraph node:

strong: "Consider adjusting your layout at large font sizes." + text: " When font size increases in a horizontally constrained context, inline items (like glyphs and timestamps) and container boundaries can crowd text and cause truncation or overlapping. To improve readability, consider using a stacked layout where text appears above secondary items. Multicolumn text can also be less readable at large sizes due to horizontal space constraints. Reduce the number of columns when the font size increases to avoid truncation and enhance readability."

So the supporting quote is word-for-word accurate, not paraphrased or stitched. Context: the bullet sits in the Dynamic Type best-practices run of the Typography page, immediately after "Make sure your app's layout adapts to all font sizes," "Increase the size of meaningful interface icons as font size increases," and "Keep text truncation to a minimum as font size increases."

CURRENCY: page metadata customMetadata.alert-date = "2025-12-16" ("Added emphasized weights to the Dynamic Type style specifications for each platform"), supported-platforms ios,ipados,macos,tvos,visionos,watchos — i.e. this is the live, recently-maintained page as of 2026-08-01, not an archived HIG. Independent search corroboration returned the same sentence, plus an older/looser HIG wording ("At large font sizes, an inline layout might cause text to truncate...consider using a stacked layout"), showing this guidance has persisted across HIG revisions rather than being a one-off. No source disputes or qualifies it.

ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT: "stacked (vertical)" is a fair gloss of "text appears above secondary items"; "inline glyphs, timestamps and container boundaries" maps exactly onto "inline items (like glyphs and timestamps) and container boundaries"; "crowd text and cause truncation or overlap in horizontally constrained contexts" is verbatim.

ONE QUALIFICATION (not fatal, but downstream copy should not harden it): Apple's modality is advisory — "Consider adjusting…", "consider using a stacked layout" — not a mandate. The claim's "explicitly instructs designers to switch" overstates the verb slightly. The guidance is explicit and unambiguous, and the whole HIG is advisory by construction, so the substance holds; but "Apple recommends considering a stacked layout" is the defensible phrasing, and "requires/instructs" should not be used if the claim is later cited as a hard rule.

### [2] Apple's HIG accessibility page sets an explicit text-enlargement target designers must design for: at least 200 percent enlargement (140 percent on watchOS), achievable either through custom UI or by adopting Dynamic Type.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility (primary)
Quote: "**Support larger text sizes.** Make sure people can adjust the size of your text or icons to make them more legible, visible, and comfortable to read. Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least 200 percent (or 140 percent in watchOS apps). Your interface can support font size enlargement either through custom UI, or by adopting Dynamic Type."
Verifier evidence (high): VERIFIED VERBATIM against the primary source, not a paraphrase. WebFetch failed (Apple HIG is JS-rendered), so I pulled the page's backing JSON directly: `curl https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility.json` → HTTP 200, 88,675 bytes, identifier `doc://com.apple.HIG/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/accessibility`. Grepping the JSON returns exactly one hit for "200", one for "custom UI", one for "larger text", inside a single bolded bullet in the "Vision" section (anchor `#Vision`, immediately after "The people who use your interface may be blind, color blind, or have low vision or light sensitivity"):

"**Support larger text sizes.** Make sure people can adjust the size of your text or icons to make them more legible, visible, and comfortable to read. Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least 200 percent (or 140 percent in watchOS apps). Your interface can support font size enlargement either through custom UI, or by adopting Dynamic Type."

Every load-bearing element of the claim matches character-for-character: the 200 percent floor, the 140 percent watchOS carve-out, and the explicit either/or of custom UI vs. Dynamic Type. The supporting quote as given in the claim is not fabricated or reconstructed.

CURRENCY: the page's own Change log table (extracted from the same JSON) is topped by "June 9, 2025 — Added guidance and links for Assistive Access, Switch Control, and Accessibility Nutrition Labels," preceded by "March 7, 2025 — Expanded and refined all guidance. Moved Dynamic Type guidance to the Typography page, and moved VoiceOver guidance to a new VoiceOver page." So this bullet survived the most recent full rewrite of the page and is live as fetched today (2026-08-01). Not outdated.

CORROBORATION (independent Apple primary source, not vendor content): developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria — the Accessibility Nutrition Labels "Larger Text" criteria — independently states apps must let "users enlarge text to at least 200% or the maximum font size for the system," confirms watchOS's largest Dynamic Type size exceeds 140% of default and that support may be shown "by implementing Dynamic Type or by supporting an equivalent or larger size for body text," and explicitly permits non-Dynamic-Type custom implementations (citing Apple Books, which reflows two columns to one at large sizes). Two independent Apple primary sources agree on both numbers and on the two-path implementation.

ONE QUALIFIER, not fatal: Apple's word is "Ideally," which frames the 200%/140% figure as a strong recommendation, not a hard mandate. The claim's "designers must design for" is marginally stronger than the HIG's own hedge. It is not an overreach in substance, however — the claim's operative assertion is that the HIG "sets an explicit text-enlargement target," which it demonstrably does, and the App Store Connect criteria page converts the same numbers into a pass/fail evaluation threshold for any app declaring Larger Text support, which supplies the "must" the HIG softens. A downstream writer should attribute the number as Apple's stated target while preserving "ideally."

No contradicting source found. Source is the exact primary source the research brief prioritizes (developer.apple.com HIG accessibility page); no law-firm or vendor content involved.

### [3] Apple's recommended minimum control size for iOS/iPadOS is 44x44 pt default with a 28x28 pt hard minimum — a per-platform table (macOS 28x28/20x20, tvOS 66x66/56x56, visionOS 60x60/28x28, watchOS 44x44/28x28) that differs from Android's 48dp recommendation and from any single web-derived target rule.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility (primary)
Quote: "| Platform | Default control size | Minimum control size |
| iOS, iPadOS | 44x44 pt | 28x28 pt |
| macOS | 28x28 pt | 20x20 pt |
| tvOS | 66x66 pt | 56x56 pt |
| visionOS | 60x60 pt | 28x28 pt |
| watchOS | 44x44 pt | 28x28 pt |"
Verifier evidence (high): VERBATIM CONFIRMED on the primary source, live today (2026-08-01). WebFetch returns nothing (JS-rendered), so I pulled Apple's own DocC JSON backing the page: `curl https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility.json` → HTTP 200, 88,675 bytes. Under the "Mobility" H2, the prose reads: "**Offer sufficiently sized controls.** Controls that are too small are hard for many people to interact with and select. Strive to meet the recommended minimum control size for each platform to ensure controls and menus are comfortable for all when tapping and clicking." Immediately following is a `"type": "table", "header": "row"` whose cells decode to exactly: Platform / Default control size / Minimum control size — iOS, iPadOS 44x44 pt / 28x28 pt; macOS 28x28 pt / 20x20 pt; tvOS 66x66 pt / 56x56 pt; visionOS 60x60 pt / 28x28 pt; watchOS 44x44 pt / 28x28 pt. Every number in the claim matches character-for-character. Adjacent (also usable): "add about 12 points of padding around elements that include a bezel. For elements without a bezel, about 24 points of padding works well around the element's visible edges."

Comparative tail also verified primary: developer.android.com/guide/topics/ui/accessibility/apps — "we recommend that each interactive UI element have a focusable area, or touch target size, of at least 48dpx48dp. Larger is even better." So the Apple-vs-Android divergence the claim asserts is real.

TWO QUALIFICATIONS the downstream write-up MUST carry, or it will mislead designers:
(1) "hard minimum" is the claimant's gloss, not Apple's. Apple's verb is "Strive to meet" — aspirational floor, not an enforced one. Drop "hard".
(2) The table measures *control size*; it does NOT replace the 44x44 pt *hit region* rule, and Apple still publishes that rule elsewhere. developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons (fetched same way, HTTP 200) says verbatim: "As a general rule, a button needs a hit region of at least 44x44 pt — in visionOS, 60x60 pt — to ensure that people can select it easily, whether they use a fingertip, a pointer, their eyes, or a remote." Note the visionOS conflict in particular: accessibility table says minimum 28x28 pt, Buttons page says 60x60 pt hit region. Control frame and tappable area are different measures (a 28pt glyph inside a 44pt hit region satisfies both). Android's 48dp is explicitly the *focusable/touch-target* area, so the correct like-for-like comparison is Apple 44x44 pt hit region vs Android 48dp touch target — not 28x28 vs 48dp. Claim survives; the 28x28 number must be labeled "minimum control size, not minimum tappable area."

Not marketing, not vendor content, not outdated: fetched from Apple's own docs endpoint today. The 28x28/per-platform table is recent HIG guidance (post-visionOS-era revision) — most third-party summaries still repeat only the legacy "44x44 minimum", which is why the table is worth citing, with caveat (2) attached.

### [4] Apple assigns the grouping/ordering/linking of interface elements as an explicit design responsibility, instructing designers to audit the UI for relationships that are conveyed by visual cues only (proximity, alignment) and then describe those relationships to VoiceOver.
Vote: 2-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover (primary)
Quote: "Specify how elements are grouped, ordered, or linked. Proximity, alignment, and other visible contextual cues help sighted people perceive the relationships between elements. Examine your app for places where relationships among elements are visual only. Then, describe these relationships to VoiceOver."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified verbatim against the cited primary source. developer.apple.com's HIG renders client-side, so WebFetch returned only the title; I pulled the canonical data endpoint https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover.json (HTTP 200) and found the exact text under the page's "Navigation" section, with the lead sentence marked as a bold guideline heading (JSON node type "strong"): "Specify how elements are grouped, ordered, or linked. Proximity, alignment, and other visible contextual cues help sighted people perceive the relationships between elements. Examine your app for places where relationships among elements are visual only. Then, describe these relationships to VoiceOver." Immediately following: "VoiceOver reads elements in the same order people read content in the their active language and locale. For example, in US English, this is top-to-bottom, left-to-right. In the ungrouped example below, VoiceOver describes each image before moving on to the captions. In the grouped example, VoiceOver describes each image with its respective caption," illustrated by paired assets voiceover-incorrect-grouping.png ("Ungrouped related elements make it hard for VoiceOver to accurately describe the UI", marked with crossout.png) and voiceover-correct-grouping.png ("Grouped related elements help VoiceOver accurately describe the UI", checkmark.png). Currency: page metadata change log reads "March 7, 2025 — New page," i.e. this is the current HIG page, not legacy text. Source quality matches claim strength — this IS the primary source, on the exact URL cited, not a secondary restatement. Design-vs-developer framing holds structurally: the page sits under developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/ and every item on it hands implementation off separately ("For developer guidance, see ..." appears after the labels, infographics, decorative-image, grouping, layout-change, and rotor guidelines), so the prose guidance is the design layer and the API links are the developer layer. One nit that does not rise to refutation: Apple never literally writes "designer" or "design responsibility" — it addresses a generic "you" — so "explicit design responsibility" is the claimant's (reasonable) gloss on placement in the design guidelines; the instruction to audit for visual-only relationships and describe them to VoiceOver is itself explicit and quoted correctly. No contradicting evidence is possible against a verbatim quote confirmed at the source.

### [5] The VoiceOver rotor is a navigation control that lets people move through content by headings, links, and other content types, and Apple states apps must identify those elements to the rotor for it to work; the rotor can also bring up the braille keyboard.
Vote: 1-1 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover (primary)
Quote: "Support the VoiceOver rotor when possible. People can use an interface element called the VoiceOver rotor to navigate a document or webpage by headings, links, and other content types. You can help people navigate content in your app by identifying these elements to the rotor. The rotor can also bring up the braille keyboard."
Verifier evidence (high): VERBATIM MATCH CONFIRMED ON PRIMARY SOURCE. developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover renders client-side, so I pulled its DocC payload (https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover.json, HTTP 200, 36,827 bytes) and extracted the "Navigation" section. It contains word-for-word: "Support the VoiceOver rotor when possible. People can use an interface element called the VoiceOver rotor to navigate a document or webpage by headings, links, and other content types. You can help people navigate content in your app by identifying these elements to the rotor. The rotor can also bring up the braille keyboard. For developer guidance, see [SwiftUI], [UIKit], and [AppKit]." The supporting quote is not fabricated or stitched.

CURRENCY: the same page's Change log reads "March 7, 2025 — New page." It is the current HIG VoiceOver page, well inside the 2026 scope of the research question. Not outdated.

SOURCE QUALITY: primary vendor documentation for a claim about that vendor's own platform — the highest available tier. No law-firm/vendor marketing involved.

CONTRADICTION SEARCH: found none. Apple Support corroborates independently (support.apple.com/en-us/111796 "About the VoiceOver rotor", support.apple.com/guide/iphone/control-voiceover-using-the-rotor-iph3e2e3a6d/ios, and support.apple.com/guide/iphone/type-braille-on-the-screen-iph10366cc30/ios, which confirms Braille Screen Input is reached via the rotor). App Store Connect's VoiceOver evaluation criteria page also references moving directly to parts of the screen "using features like the VoiceOver rotors."

ONE OVERREACH WORTH FLAGGING (not fatal): the claim's modality is stronger than Apple's. Apple writes "when possible" and "You can help people navigate content in your app by identifying these elements"; the claim renders this as apps "must identify those elements to the rotor for it to work." Apple frames it as a recommendation, not a requirement. The strengthened wording is nonetheless mechanically accurate for content-type navigation — the Headings rotor is driven by the app supplying the header trait, and custom rotors require accessibilityRotor / accessibilityRotorEntry (SwiftUI) or UIAccessibilityCustomRotor (UIKit), per the developer links Apple attaches to that very paragraph. It is NOT accurate for system rotor items: Braille Screen Input, character/word/line navigation, and speaking rate work without any app participation, so "must identify elements for it to work" should not be read as covering the braille keyboard half of the sentence. Downgrade "must" to "should, and Apple ties heading/link rotor navigation to the app exposing those elements" and the claim is exact.


## Refuted claims (for transparency)
- "Apple sets a concrete, testable commitment for surviving the largest accessibility sizes: the amount of useful text displayed at the largest accessibility font size should equal what is displayed at the largest standard font size, and truncation in scrollable regions is disallowed unless a separate full-content view exists." (https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography, vote 0-3)
## Unverified claims (18 — verifier agents failed; neither confirmed nor refuted)
- "Apple states VoiceOver reads elements in the reading order of the user's active language and locale (top-to-bottom, left-to-right in US English), which means default reading order is derived from layout — so a designer must explicitly group related elements or VoiceOver will read all images before all captions rather than pairing each image with its caption." (https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover, 2/3 votes errored)
- "Apple's Dynamic Type ramp offers 7 text sizes by default, plus 5 additional "larger accessibility sizes" when the user enables them, for 12 total sizes an app layout must survive." (https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2024/10074/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Apple's stated guidance is that horizontal layouts should dynamically switch to a vertical stack at accessibility text sizes so each element can take the full display width — a layout decision, not a font-size decision." (https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2024/10074/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Apple states that iOS Dynamic Type reaches sizes larger than 200% of the default at the AX3 accessibility size, and allows body text sizes over 300% at AX5 — giving designers concrete numeric targets for the top of the Dynamic Type ramp." (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Apple's stated layout guidance for large accessibility text sizes is that side-by-side elements should reflow — wrapping onto a new line or being laid out vertically instead of horizontally — because they overlap when enlarged." (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Apple's criteria treat truncation as a failure condition at large text sizes: text must not truncate to the point of being unreadable or ambiguous, and the recommended remedy is wrapping to two or more lines." (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Apple explicitly disallows relying on system-provided magnification (Zoom, Hover Text) to satisfy the Larger Text requirement — the app's own layout must scale, which is a native-specific requirement with no direct web-checklist equivalent (browser zoom/reflow is normally an acceptable web mechanism under WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10)." (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Apple's App Store Connect VoiceOver evaluation criteria require a separate accessibility label distinct from the value for interactive form controls — the label names the field, the value carries its contents." (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/voiceover-evaluation-criteria/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Apple explicitly prohibits encoding control type or state inside the accessibility label, and requires that information to be carried by accessibility traits instead — labels that duplicate the type produce doubled speech such as "checkbox, checkbox."" (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/voiceover-evaluation-criteria/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Apple's criteria require every visible element to be reachable both linearly (swipe/VO+Arrow) and via the VoiceOver rotor, require the user to be able to navigate away from any element, and require that forward and backward traversal never skip items or loop repeatedly." (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/voiceover-evaluation-criteria/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "For grouped elements, Apple gives designers a binary choice: either each item in the group is individually navigable, or the grouped behaviors are exposed as VoiceOver custom actions (e.g. reply, forward, delete on a single grouped row)." (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/voiceover-evaluation-criteria/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Android 14 raised the maximum user font scale to 200%, and applies a nonlinear scaling curve so large text scales less aggressively than small text — preserving type hierarchy and preventing cut-off or unreadably large display text." (https://developer.android.com/about/versions/14/features, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Because scaling is nonlinear, sp dimensions are no longer additive — 4sp + 20sp does not necessarily equal 24sp — so sp must not be used for padding or for view heights that assume implicit padding." (https://developer.android.com/about/versions/14/features, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Text sizes must be specified in sp units for the user's preferred text size to apply at all; apps using sp get the Android 14 scaling improvements automatically, but must still be UI-tested at the 200% maximum." (https://developer.android.com/about/versions/14/features, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Android's official design guidance sets a minimum touch target of 48 dp, and explicitly requires that minimum be met even when it exceeds the visible bounds of the UI element." (https://developer.android.com/design/ui/mobile/guides/foundations/accessibility, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Android requires font sizes to be declared in scalable pixels (sp) so user font-size settings apply, and sets a floor of 12 sp for body text aligned to the Material type scale." (https://developer.android.com/design/ui/mobile/guides/foundations/accessibility, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Android's designer-facing accessibility guidance requires textual descriptions for icons and images, and requires decorative items to have their description set to null so screen readers skip them — a labelling decision distinct from web alt-text conventions." (https://developer.android.com/design/ui/mobile/guides/foundations/accessibility, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Android's official accessibility principles require designers/developers to mark heading elements semantically (the `heading` property in the `semantics` modifier), because accessibility-service users can then jump between headings instead of paragraphs or words — Android's structural-navigation analogue to the iOS VoiceOver rotor." (https://developer.android.com/guide/topics/ui/accessibility/principles, 3/3 votes errored)

Mention in caveats that 18 claim(s) could not be verified due to infrastructure errors.

## Instructions
1. Identify claims that say the same thing — merge them, combine their sources.
2. Group related claims into coherent findings. Each finding should directly address the research question.
3. Assign confidence per finding: high (multiple primary sources, unanimous votes), medium (secondary sources or split votes), low (single source or blog-quality).
4. Write a 3-5 sentence executive summary answering the research question.
5. Note caveats: what's uncertain, what sources were weak, what time-sensitivity applies.
6. List 2-4 open questions that emerged but weren't answered.

Structured output only.

{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"SubagentStart","additionalContext":"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.

4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it

Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files.
